name: Scrap-Stitch Patchwork Tank
description:
Not a product with a brand — a category of garment that exists across the Shelf wherever people have access to a needle, thread, and discarded fabric. This particular style has emerged as something almost coherent: a tank top constructed from three to six different fabric panels, each from a different source — a piece of a Caldero thermal, a strip of printed synthwool, a section of what might have been a corporate uniform, all sewn together with visible stitching in mismatched thread colors. Some makers reinforce stress points with salvaged metal rings or knotted cord. Some add patches — hand-drawn logos, strips of reflective tape, safety pins through the hem.

What distinguishes a good scrap-stitch tank from a bad one is the stitching and the color sense. The best ones show a genuine eye for what goes together. They circulate by gift and trade as often as sale. Wearing one is a declaration of where you come from that no amount of money can buy, which is why Tier 3 and 4 youth occasionally try, and why it always reads wrong when they do.
what_it_says: You're from the Shelf, or you respect what the Shelf makes. You don't need a brand to have a look.
worn_by: anyone who grew up making do
manufacturer: Various independent Shelf makers (no unified brand)
story_hooks: A Tier 5 fashion house released a 'deconstructed patchwork' collection for Φ1,800 per piece that was clearly derived from Shelf scrap-stitch. The designer has never been to the Shelf. The Shelf noticed.

A specific maker on Level 3 of Stack 6 uses a distinctive double-stitch in orange thread that has become a kind of signature — her tanks are traded like currency. Someone has started counterfeiting the orange stitch.

A scrap-stitch tank made from pieces of three different corporate uniforms — Vantablack, TESSERA, and an unidentified third — was brought to a fixer who wants to know which facility the scraps came from and how they ended up on the Shelf.
